C005.subject: Raising the minimum wage in low-wage labor markets with monopsony power
C005.object: unemployment among low-skilled workers more strongly when combined with a binding wage floor that exceeds the monopsony wage by at least 15%
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage in low-wage labor markets with monopsony power unemployment among low-skilled workers more strongly when combined with a binding wage floor that exceeds the monopsony wage by at least 15%]

[PATH:empirical] Card and Krueger (1994) study of the New Jersey minimum wage increase and its effect on fast-food employment, reanalyzed with a focus on markets with high employer concentration (monopsony power) and wage floors exceeding monopsony levels by at least 15%. — This classic natural experiment provides a baseline for testing whether larger minimum wage increases in monopsonistic markets reduce unemployment among low-skilled workers, as the hypothesis predicts.

[PATH:empirical] Azar, Marinescu, and Steinbaum (2020) analysis of labor market concentration and minimum wage effects using online job posting data, extended to examine thresholds where the wage floor exceeds estimated monopsony wages by 15% or more. — This modern data source allows direct measurement of monopsony power across local labor markets and can test the specific 15% binding threshold condition on unemployment outcomes for low-skilled workers.

[PATH:theoretical] Bhaskar, Manning, and To (2002) theoretical model of oligopsony and minimum wages, extended to simulate the nonlinear effects of wage floors above the monopsony wage. — A formal model can clarify the conditions under which a minimum wage exceeding the monopsony wage by 15% reduces unemployment, helping to validate the causal mechanism and boundary conditions of the hypothesis.

C006.subject: Raising the minimum wage in low-wage labor markets with monopsony power
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage in low-wage labor markets with monopsony power unemployment among low-skilled workers]

[PATH:empirical] Card and Krueger (1994) 'Minimum Wages and Employment: A Case Study of the Fast-Food Industry in New Jersey and Pennsylvania' — This classic natural experiment directly tests the employment effects of a minimum wage increase in a low-wage, monopsony-prone industry. Replicating or extending this analysis with post-2000 US data could confirm or refute the hypothesis, as it provides a benchmark for estimating unemployment effects under monopsony.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review of US minimum wage studies from 2000 onward (e.g., meta-analyses by Doucouliagos and Stanley, 2009, or updated versions) — A comprehensive meta-analysis of post-2000 empirical studies on minimum wage and low-skilled employment in the US would aggregate evidence across many contexts, clarifying whether the hypothesized positive unemployment effect holds on average or is null/negative, especially in markets with monopsony power.

[PATH:theoretical] Structural estimation of monopsony models using firm-level wage and employment data (e.g., Manning, 2003 'Monopsony in Motion') — Developing or applying a structural model that estimates the degree of monopsony power in specific low-wage US labor markets (e.g., retail, hospitality) would allow direct testing of whether minimum wage increases reduce employment under measured monopsony conditions, providing a causal mechanism check.

C007.subject: Raising the minimum wage in high-competition, low-margin industries
C007.object: unemployment among low-skilled workers more when the wage hike is large and sudden than when it is phased in gradually
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage in high-competition, low-margin industries unemployment among low-skilled workers more when the wage hike is large and sudden than when it is phased in gradually]

[PATH:empirical] Natural experiment comparing U.S. states that enacted large, sudden minimum wage increases (e.g., Washington D.C.'s jump to $15) with states that phased in similar increases over multiple years (e.g., California's gradual schedule), using CPS or QCEW data to estimate employment effects on low-skilled workers in retail and food services. — Directly tests the hypothesis by contrasting sudden vs. gradual wage hikes in high-turnover, low-margin industries, controlling for local economic conditions and pre-existing trends.

[PATH:theoretical] Structural labor demand model calibrated to low-margin industries (e.g., fast food) that simulates firm responses to different wage-increase trajectories, incorporating adjustment costs, attrition rates, and productivity pass-through. — Provides a causal mechanism: if gradual hikes allow firms to substitute capital or improve efficiency without immediate layoffs, the model will predict lower unemployment under phased increases, confirming the hypothesis.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of minimum wage studies (e.g., Doucouliagos & Stanley, 2009) that codes each study's policy timing (sudden vs. phased) and industry competitiveness, then tests whether effect sizes on low-skilled employment differ by implementation speed. — Synthesizes existing evidence to see if the hypothesized pattern holds across multiple contexts, addressing generalizability and publication bias.

qualifier.note: A rapid jump in labor costs forces firms to immediately cut payroll, whereas gradual increases allow adjustment through attrition and productivity gains.

C008.subject: Raising the minimum wage in high-competition, low-margin industries
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage in high-competition, low-margin industries economic growth and job creation]

[PATH:empirical] Meta-analysis of minimum wage studies focusing on low-margin industries (e.g., fast food, retail) using border discontinuity designs (e.g., Card & Krueger 1994, subsequent replications) — Directly tests employment and growth effects in high-competition, low-margin sectors by comparing contiguous regions with different minimum wage levels, controlling for local economic shocks.

[PATH:theoretical] Dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) model incorporating firm heterogeneity, market power, and wage floors — Models the general equilibrium effects of minimum wage hikes in competitive low-margin industries, capturing potential trade-offs between wage increases, firm exit, and aggregate demand that empirical studies may miss.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal firm-level data from the U.S. Census Bureau (e.g., Longitudinal Business Database) tracking employment, revenue, and survival rates of low-margin firms pre- and post-2010 minimum wage increases — Provides granular evidence on job creation and economic growth at the firm level, allowing identification of heterogeneous effects across high-competition industries and controlling for selection bias.
